22.0.s.en: (1) The parable of the wedding feast

22.0.0.en: As was Christ's custom, He presented the spiritual meanings in parables so that they would be close to the understanding of His hearers, because of the hardness of their hearts and their inclination to reject His teachings that were deep spiritually.

22.0.2.en: "A wedding": the Church, in which God rejoices in the union of His people with Him, by partaking of His most holy Body and Blood, as they receive salvation from sin through Baptism, confession and Communion.

22.1.0.en: "Sent forth his servants": the Fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the prophets, and all the men of the Old Testament who made God known to mankind.

22.1.1.en: "Other servants": the Apostles and disciples, and the priests and servants of the New Testament, who call mankind to faith and to life in the Church.

22.1.2.en: God respects the will of man, so He calls him to His Church and does not force him. He has prepared everything, and He offers us His love, and it remains for us to respond to Him.

22.1.3.en: "They would not come": that is, the Jews rejected the teachings of the prophets, kept away from repentance, and did not believe in Christ. "My oxen and my fatlings are killed": this refers to the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which the sacrifices of the Old Testament were a type of, and which is the sacrifice of His Body and Blood on the altar every day.

22.1.4.en: It also signifies the word of God, which satisfies the soul.

22.1.5.en: Likewise it signifies the life of the martyrs and the saints, who offered their lives as a sacrifice of love for God after the example of the crucified Christ, and whose lives satisfy the believing soul with the love of God put into practice in their lives.

22.2.0.en: Sadly, the response of those who were invited to the one who gave the wedding was bad, for they were absorbed in material desires, which are expressed by the farm and the merchandise. They signify the Jews, who had the promises and the call to life with God, but were absorbed in material things; and more than this, they mistreated His prophets who carried His invitation to them, and they insulted them and killed them.

22.3.0.en: "The king": he is God. He was angry at the evils of those who were invited, and issued his command to destroy them, that is, eternal torment for their refusal to believe, as well as the destruction of their city, which indeed happened in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed the city of Jerusalem.

22.4.1.en: "As many as ye shall find": the invitation is for all mankind.

22.4.2.en: The Jews rejected God's invitation, though they should have been an example of faith before the Gentiles, so God directed His invitation to the whole world through His servants the disciples and Apostles. They went out into the ways of the world calling everyone to faith and to the feast of Christ, that is, His most holy Body and Blood.

22.5.0.en: "Bad": their past life was full of evils that were visible before people.

22.5.1.en: "Good": they have virtues known before others.

22.5.2.en: But all need faith in Christ and His redemption, and repentance from their sins.

22.5.3.en: The disciples called all the Gentiles, whether the bad among them or the good, however great the sins of the bad, provided they were ready to repent. So they believed and left their past life, and entered the Church believing in Christ, to be satisfied by Him.

22.6.0.en: "A wedding garment": clothes that the giver of the wedding provides to the invited. Here it signifies the Holy Sacraments, especially Baptism, confession and Communion. If someone neglects these garments and relies on his own righteousness, that is, does not continue in confession and Communion and in walking in the new life with God, he is stripped of the wedding garments, and his end is destruction.

22.6.1.en: So when the Gentiles believed and entered the Church, they had to keep their lives pure in God by continuing in a life of repentance, so that they would have the pure life, which is the garment fitting for the wedding, that is, being in the Church on earth and then extending in it forever.

22.7.0.en: Then the hour of judgment comes, and the king, that is, God, asks the negligent among the believers: how did you not abide in His love and the love of others, especially enemies? How did you make light of sins and not repent of them? Then these wicked ones fall silent, because there is no longer time for repentance.

22.8.0.en: The negligent person binds his life with sin, and so receives his recompense, which is to be bound to it forever for torment, because he rejected the freedom of the Spirit and the enjoyment of God.

22.8.1.en: The severity of the torment, and the body's sharing in it with the soul after it has been changed into a spiritual body, is expressed by "weeping and gnashing of teeth", and this means very severe pains.

22.9.0.en: Thus God calls everyone to faith, but those who believe and remain steadfast in faith are few, and these are the chosen for eternal life.

22.9.1.en: † The opportunity of a lifetime allows you to take part in the Lord's supper, that is, to partake of the Holy Sacraments. So do not let the engagements of life distract you from it, and do not excuse yourself from it because of the multitude of your sins, for the sacrament of confession forgives you everything, however hard it was or however long it has dominated you for many years.

22.9.2.en: So do not be negligent, forgetting your sins, but take care to put on the wedding garment, so that you may eat of the king's supper. Persevere in that, and you will rejoice in fellowship with Christ and live with Him forever.

22.10.0.en: "The Herodians": a group of Jews who sided with the family of Herod, which was of Edomite origin, that is, not Jewish, and who hoped that a member of this family would be governor of Judea on behalf of the Roman authority, and who were concerned with submission to the Roman state and the collection of tribute.

22.10.1.en: The Pharisees continued in their evil toward Christ. Although they despised the Herodians because they followed the Roman authority, while they themselves resisted the Roman occupier, they united with them in order to catch Christ in some error. In hypocrisy, they praised Christ, saying that He was a teacher of truth, and provoked Him by their praise of Him that He fears no one, so that He would refuse to pay the tribute. Then they asked Him: is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar according to the commands of the Roman state? If He said it is given, He would be cooperating with the occupier, and they would stir up the Jews against Him. And if He said no, He would become a resister of the state, and He would have to be arrested and tried.

22.10.2.en: "Caesar": the name of any Roman emperor, like the title Pharaoh for any king in ancient Egypt, and the Caesar at that time was Tiberius.

22.11.0.en: God, who searches the hearts and knows the unseen, knew their thoughts, and said to them: "Why tempt ye me?" He warned them of their sin, which is hypocrisy, that perhaps they would repent and believe in Him as God who knows the unseen, but sadly they were not moved, because of the hardness of their hearts.

22.12.0.en: "Shew me the tribute money": this is one of the kinds of money with which the tribute is paid, such as the Roman denarius. By presenting this denarius, the Pharisees declared their submission to the authority, contrary to what they proclaim, that their submission must be to the Temple only. They did not have only Jewish money, such as the shekel, but Roman money as well. So He showed them that they proclaim what they do not practice, out of fear of the authority.

22.12.1.en: Christ asked them for one of the coins, and they showed Him a denarius that of course had the image of the Roman Caesar and his name. He asked them: whose is this image and superscription? They said: Caesar's. He said to them: render to Caesar what is his, which is the tribute and all the political duties required of a citizen of the Roman state; since the state provides services to its citizens, it deserves to receive this tribute. But what is more important, which is the spirit, give to God, because money is the lowest and least important, whereas the spirit of man is the most important thing in him. They marvelled greatly at His wisdom, because He did not fall into an error that they could hold against Him, but sadly they did not believe and repent.

22.12.2.en: You are the image of God, so give Him your heart and your life, and do not be an image of the devil by loving evil desires and pride. Repent and cleave to God, so that you may regain His image in you.

22.13.0.en: The Sadducees were a wealthy aristocratic sect of the Jews, who did not believe in another life after this world, or in a resurrection of bodies after their decomposition, and most of the high priests were from among them.

22.14.0.en: The Sadducees referred to Christ to a part of the Law of Moses, namely that if a man married a woman and died without having children, his brother or nearest kinsman would marry her after him, so as to raise up seed in the name of the dead man, to inherit his land and preserve it, and the firstborn son would be ascribed to the dead man (Deut 25:6), and that was a symbol of preserving our eternal inheritance.

22.15.0.en: They composed a story and asked Christ about it, since they saw it as a dilemma with no solution. It was of seven brothers, one of whom married a woman and died without children, so the second married her and likewise had no children, and so on until the seventh brother, and he had no children, and then the woman died. Their question was: if there is a resurrection and eternal life, to which of the seven will this wife belong, to live with him in eternity, since she had been the wife of all of them on earth, and bore no children, so that no one could answer them that she would be the wife of the one by whom she had borne children.

22.16.0.en: Christ pointed out to them their lack of care and their lack of understanding of the prophecies of the prophets, for they always took them in the material sense, because their thinking was immersed in material things, though the speech is clear about a spiritual life in heaven, and no need for bodily relations or any material work, but all will be spirits attached to God, gathered by feelings of love without distinction of bodily kinship, for they have risen above it by their deep spiritual sense. And because they are immortal, they do not need marriage and procreation; they know one another as spirits, without need of bodily feelings.

22.17.0.en: Christ gave them another proof besides the prophecies of the Holy Scriptures, namely God's saying to Moses and to the prophets that He is the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Ex 3:6 and 15). Would God ascribe Himself to dead men who have come to an end and no longer have any worth?!

22.17.1.en: Of course not. For the great God ascribes Himself to spirits alive with Him in heaven who are His children, whom we knew in the body and who now live by the spirit in heaven.

22.17.2.en: He brought this proof from the books of Moses because the Sadducees rely on them and neglect many other books of the Old Testament. For God did not say "I was the God of Abraham", but He is their God at present. And this was in His speaking with Moses many years after their death, which means that their spirits are alive in heaven, and He is their God; spirits do not vanish with the death of the body, as the Sadducees proclaim.

22.18.0.en: Because of the loftiness of Christ's teachings, His wisdom and the power of His words, the hearers were astonished, and the Sadducees were silenced before His argument. The multitudes were not only of the Sadducees, but also of the Pharisees and ordinary Jews.

22.18.1.en: Think of the greatness of heaven and the glory of the spirits there, so that you may not be immersed in material desires, but reject your evils and care for your spiritual life.

22.19.0.en: The Sadducees lost the ability to catch Christ in any error, or even to converse with Him, because of His strong argument. So the Pharisees, who hold fast to the Law, gathered together to tempt Christ and make Him fall into some error.

22.19.1.en: The power of God that is in you silences the wicked, however great their evils or their schemes, because God who is with you is stronger than all the demons who stir up evil in men.

22.20.0.en: A Pharisee among them, who was a lawyer, that is, one of those exacting in keeping and expounding the commandments and the Law of Moses, asked Christ: which is the great commandment? So that if Christ singled out one of them, He would be in error, because all are commandments of God. Perhaps they had heard of His Sermon on the Mount, in which He completed the meanings of the commandments, so that they might accuse Him of saying that the Law is deficient.

22.20.1.en: Are you innocent in your speech with others, or do you try to show your own distinction or their weaknesses?

22.21.0.en: Christ summed up the Ten Commandments in two commandments, and did not single out one above the other. The first commandment speaks of man's relation to God, that he love Him with all his being, that is, with his heart, soul and mind, and this is the most important thing, namely the love of God, and from it necessarily results the second commandment, which is love of the neighbor, that is, all mankind, and it is proof of man's love for God.

22.21.1.en: True love is a person's love for the other as for himself, not merely some concern, and then the love of the New Testament grows greater, so that loving the other becomes more than loving oneself, as Christ did on the Cross, for He loved us and gave Himself for us.

22.21.2.en: Not only this, but out of the overflow of the river of His love that never runs dry, and at the height of the sufferings, He asked the Father for those who crucified Him, saying: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).

22.22.0.en: By this love, all the Law and the commandments and the words of the prophets are summed up.

22.23.0.en: Christ was longsuffering toward the questions of the Sadducees, the Pharisees and the lawyers, some of which were mentioned in the preceding verses, and their attempt to make Him fall into any error. And He silenced them with His strong arguments. In the end, He was compelled to show them the error of what they were doing, for by this they were resisting the truth, and they were very weak before it, so He asked them a religious question from their study of the prophets and the Law, namely: what do the Holy Scriptures say about the expected Messiah, whose son is He? They quickly answered: "The Son of David", for there is no dispute about that, that He would come from the seed of David according to the prophecies.

22.24.0.en: "Doth David call him": in (Ps 110:1), and the Jews were agreed that its writer was David. "In spirit": by divine inspiration.

22.24.2.en: "My Lord": that is, the master and God of David, and a man cannot call his son or grandson "my Lord". Christ said to them: if He is the son of David, how does David in his psalm call Him his Lord, when he said: "The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand" (Ps 110:1)? And that is in a conversation between the Father and the Son after Christ completes redemption on the Cross, and all the demons become subject to Him, for He bound them with His Cross, that is, He comes to be in His divine majesty, which is indicated by the right hand.

22.24.3.en: How then can He be the son of David and the Lord of David at the same time?!

22.25.0.en: The Pharisees were bewildered and unable to answer, because they were absorbed in material thinking about Christ, though the answer is simple, understood by any Christian, namely that Christ is the son of David in the flesh, and is the eternal God at the same time, for He is God incarnate.

22.25.1.en: And since they felt their inability, they departed from Him in shame, and no longer resisted Him.

22.25.2.en: God wants you not to resist the truth, but to repent and love Him and live with Him; so obey the word of God and live in it. The twenty-third: the pride of the Pharisees; the formality of worship.
